title: Brenda Blethyn Asks If Vera Is Worth Watching One Last Time
metaDescription: Brenda Blethyn asks fans to be honest: is Vera worth watching? Rate the ITV crime drama from 1 to 10 as the final episodes air.
author: Mia Carter
altText: Brenda Blethyn as DCI Vera Stanhope on the Northumberland coast in the ITV crime drama Vera
html:
Brenda Blethyn has a blunt question for anyone who has spent the past fourteen years watching her solve murders on the Northumberland coast. Is Vera worth watching? She is not asking for praise. She wants honesty, and she wants a number.

The actress behind DCI Vera Stanhope posted the question on Facebook, asking viewers to rate the show on a scale of 1 to 10. It is a simple request from a woman who has carried one of British television's most enduring detectives for well over a decade. No hype, no trailer, no announcement. Just a straight question to the people who actually watch.

For anyone who has somehow missed it, Vera is the ITV crime drama built around Ann Cleeves' novels. Blethyn plays the title character, a scruffy, sharp-tongued detective chief inspector who works the windswept north-east of England. The show has been a fixture of Sunday-night television since 2011.

Why Brenda Blethyn Is Asking If Vera Is Worth Watching

There is a timing reason behind the question. The series wrapped its run with a final set of episodes, bringing Vera Stanhope's story to a close after thirteen series. So when Blethyn asks whether Vera is worth watching, she is asking about a body of work that has now ended, not a show still chasing new seasons.

That changes the tone of the question. A star mid-run usually wants ratings, headlines, a renewal. A star at the end wants a verdict. Blethyn has spent years in that mac and hat, and she knows the audience that stuck with her. Asking them to score the whole thing from 1 to 10 is closer to a curtain call than a marketing push.

What Makes the ITV Crime Drama Stand Out

Vera Stanhope is not a glossy detective. She does not wear tailored coats or deliver clever one-liners in a spotless incident room. She is untidy, impatient, and often the smartest person in any room she walks into. That contrast is the engine of the show.

The setting does a lot of quiet work too. The Northumberland coastline gives the series a cold, open, windblown feel that most crime dramas never manage. Blethyn has said in the past that she loves filming there, and it shows. The landscape is practically a supporting character.

Then there is the supporting cast. Kenny Doughty, Jon Morrison, and the rotating team around Vera gave the show a lived-in feel. Fans grew attached to the sidekicks almost as much as the detective herself.

The Real Reason the Question Lands

Brenda Blethyn is not a newcomer asking for attention. She has been working in film, television, and theatre since the 1970s. She earned an Oscar nomination for Secrets & Lies, picked up a Golden Globe, and built a career that most actors would trade almost anything for.

So when a performer at that level asks whether Vera is worth watching, it is not insecurity. It is curiosity from someone who knows the audience and wants to hear from them directly. Few stars with her résumé bother to ask.

There is also a broader shift at play. Long-running British crime dramas have been ending or pausing more often in recent years. When a show like Vera closes, it takes a piece of Sunday-night routine with it. Blethyn's question lands right in that gap.

Should You Rate Vera on a Scale of 1 to 10?

If you have watched even a handful of episodes, you probably already have a number in mind. Maybe it is a solid 8 for the writing, or a 9 for Blethyn alone. Maybe the later series lost something for you, and you would land closer to a 6.

That is the point. Blethyn is not asking for a fan club vote. She is asking viewers to be honest, which is a rare thing for a star of her standing to do.

If you have not seen the ITV crime drama, the question is a fair prompt to start. The early series hold up well, and Blethyn's performance is the reason the show lasted as long as it did. Whether you land on a 5 or a 10, she wants to hear it.

So go ahead. Be honest. Give her the number.
